description: We’re a group of passionate and tech-driven students from CCU, Taiwan, excited to explore AI, space science, and real-world problems together! We’re interested in using NASA’s microgravity combustion data to build something meaningful and innovative for future spaceflight safety. We welcome curious and collaborative teammates who are excited to work together, share ideas, learn new things, and contribute their skills.
summary:
FlameGuard is an interactive dashboard for the NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge Flame in Freefall. A habitat designer selects a cabin and a witness material. The page compares that cabin with NASA’s published microgravity combustion record and keeps measured numbers separate from screening math.

The comparison the challenge needs is this: in Olson and Ferkul, AIAA 2012-3492, Table I, the upward limiting oxygen of Nomex, Ultem, and Mylar is lower at lunar or Martian gravity than at 1 g. A NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 pass at Earth gravity is not the worst published case. Saffire-VI has burned a large fire near 34 percent oxygen and 8.2 psia only in microgravity. That atmosphere at lunar or Martian gravity and vehicle scale has not been flown.

Mission states the limit. Atlas ranks BASS, Saffire, SAME, FLEX, ACME, and the partial-gravity table for the selected cabin. Ember answers a question only from cited rows. The brief prints the same state. FlameGuard does not certify a material or a vehicle, and it is not a NASA product.
details:
FlameGuard lets a habitat designer set a cabin — oxygen, pressure, forced flow, and gravity — and a witness material, then read that cabin against NASA’s published combustion record.

Mission gives the published limiting oxygen for Nomex, Ultem, or Mylar and an exposure index. The index is the unweighted mean of four scores from 0 to 100: limit, oxygen fraction, detection, and suppression. It ranks cabins. It is not a probability of fire. For Nomex, ISS air at 21% is the only Guarded case. Exploration air, 34% oxygen at 8.2 psia, is above the published limit at every gravity in the table. Mars has the larger Nomex limit overrun. Deep-space transit has the higher index, because detection and suppression are harder in free fall with no resupply.

Atlas ranks BASS, Saffire I–VI, SAME, FLEX, ACME, the Olson and Ferkul gravity table, OCHMO-TB-008, and FM2. The score is gravity match, plus distance to the nearest published test atmosphere, plus overlap with the hazard that cabin is raising. FM2 stays visible for a lunar exploration-air question and is reduced by 10 points because it is a planned payload.

Ember retrieves cited findings and writes the answer from those rows. It does not call an outside language model. A question with no overlap returns a thin confidence instead of a guess. The brief prints the limit, the 1 g gap, detection, suppression, spread, the open cell, and the method.

The dashboard is a static Vite, React, and TypeScript site. Session state stays in the browser. Source: https://github.com/aykumar21/FlameGuard

Built by Ayush Kumar, Naisha Eshwar Shelke, and Chandana Virupaksha at National Chung Cheng University. Independent Space Apps project. Not a NASA product and not a flight certification.
dataRefs: Olson and Ferkul 2012, AIAA 2012-3492, Table I
Saffire spread rates, Combustion and Flame 2022, Table 1
FLEX cool flames, Nayagam et al. 2012
FM2, Flammability of Materials on the Moon, NTRS 20240015307
NASA, Studying Combustion and Fire Safety, including ACME BRE
